<reason>Side B built a more complete, adaptive, and mechanistically persuasive case. First, Side B completely neutralized Side A's primary practical harm—that animal-style review would bottleneck Alzheimer's and ALS research—by pointing out that passive disease-modeling organoids do not undergo closed-loop learning and would never trigger oversight, a point Side A quietly dropped after the first rebuttal. Second, while Side A repeatedly insisted that organoids cannot suffer without peripheral nociceptors, thalamocortical loops, and a brainstem, Side B effectively explained that microelectrode arrays bypass peripheral nerves to deliver disruptive electrical stimulation directly to central human neural tissue, and that waiting for dish-bound cultures to grow peripheral nerves or brainstems sets an impossible threshold for precaution. Finally, Side B demonstrated concretely how the Three Rs apply to closed-loop stimulation protocols and neatly turned Side A's warning about regulating computer algorithms into the literal definition of Replacement.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In Closing [B5.3], Side B dismantled Side A's slippery-slope claim that triggering review at learning would force committees to regulate computer algorithms [A4.4], pointing out that the trigger applies only to biological organoids and that swapping living cultures for computer algorithms is literally Replacement—the first pillar of the Three Rs.</best_rebuttal>
